lesson.title: Richtung II: hinten, Norden, Osten, Westen, Süden
lesson.subtitle: behind, and the four compass points — dawn, evening, sun-side and the left hand

hook.title: One Body Word, Four Sky Words
hook.content: Five direction words — one for your body, four for the sky. hinten is the body word: German built it on the same ancient behind-root that gave English behind (be-hind, 'by the hind part') — and the t in hinten is German's old directional suffix, not the D→T shift: the shift never touches this word, behind simply kept the d. English keeps the hin family only in the archaic-sounding hence and hither; German still says hin every day — hin und her, back and forth. The four compass points are pure twins, because German and English read the same sky. der Norden ↔ north. der Osten ↔ east — from the dawn-word *austrōn, 'toward the sunrise', the same dawn-root Latin turned into aurora. der Süden ↔ south — from *sunþrą, literally 'the sun side', the warm side of the sky. der Westen ↔ west — from the evening-root Latin keeps in vesper. Four sky twins, one body twin, and a lesson you can navigate by.

footnotes.title: North Is a Left-Handed Word
footnotes.content: Norden is the odd one out: it is not a sun word. The old root *ner- meant 'left' — face the rising sun and north is your left hand. East is where you look at dawn, west where the evening glow goes (Latin vesper and English west are the same evening-word), and south is the sun side. One compass, four etymologies.

pattern.title: The Compass Takes der, hinten Takes Nothing
pattern.content: Compass points are masculine and take im: im Norden, im Osten, im Süden, im Westen — 'in the north'. Motion adds the accusative: in den Süden, or plain nach Süden ('southward'). hinten is an adverb — no article, no case: hinten links (at the back on the left), von hinten (from behind), hinten im Garten (at the back of the garden). The fronting frame from Richtung I still holds: put a place in position 1 and the verb holds slot 2 — Im Süden ist es warm. And the compass scales into real sentences: Der Zug kommt aus dem Osten — the train comes from the east.
pattern.linguist_note: English behind is literally 'by the hind part' — the same hind that survives in hind legs and hindquarters. German kept the whole family alive: hinten, hinter, hintereinander. English kept the adjective and the preposition; German kept the everyday adverb.

exercises.prompt: The compass and the space behind you — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The garden is at the back on the left
The train comes from the east
matching_pairs.german: Der Zug kommt aus dem Osten

matching_pairs.english: The bridge is in the south
There are four streets in the north
matching_pairs.german: Es gibt vier Straßen im Norden

matching_pairs.english: The church is in the west
Go straight ahead, not to the right
matching_pairs.german: Gehen Sie geradeaus, nicht nach rechts

exercises.target_answer: Der Garten ist hinten links, Das Auto kommt von hinten, Der Zug kommt aus dem Osten, Die Brücke ist im Süden, Es gibt vier Straßen im Norden, Die Kirche ist im Westen, Gehen Sie geradeaus, nicht nach rechts
exercises.explanation: hinten needs no article; the compass points take im or aus dem. The frame is always the same: place phrase, verb, rest — Der Zug kommt aus dem Osten.

exercises.prompt: One of these words describes the space BEHIND you, not a point of the compass — which?
exercises.meaning: hinten = at the back, behind you — not a sky direction
exercises.explanation: hinten is where YOUR body is: hinten links, von hinten. Norden, Osten and Westen are world-fixed — they point the same way no matter how you turn. Body-relative versus sky-fixed: one word each.

exercises.prompt: Osten is the pure twin of an everyday English direction word. Which one?
exercises.explanation: Osten and east both grow from the old dawn-word *austrōn — 'toward the sunrise'; even Latin aurora (dawn) is a cousin. The compass points are world-fixed: der Osten always lies where the sun rises.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the weather-on-the-compass sentence: 'It is warm in the south'
exercises.meaning: It is warm in the south
exercises.explanation: Place first, verb second: Im Süden ist es warm. The impersonal es does the work, and the two distractor tiles show the frame scales to every compass point — Im Norden ist es kalt.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The train comes from the south at ten o'clock'
exercises.target_answer: Der Zug kommt um zehn Uhr aus dem Süden
exercises.meaning: The train comes from the south at ten o'clock
exercises.explanation: Time before place: um zehn Uhr, then aus dem Süden. The bank holds eins and vier to prove the frame takes any clock number — um eins, um vier, um zehn.

summary.outcome: Use hinten for the space behind you and the four compass points for the world's directions — im Norden, aus dem Osten, in den Süden.

use_example.german: Der Zug kommt um zehn Uhr aus dem Süden.
use_example.english: The train comes from the south at ten o'clock.

summary.takeaway: hinten is behind's twin — German built it with a t-suffix, not the D→T shift; Norden, Osten, Westen and Süden are pure sky twins — dawn, evening, sun-side and the left hand.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the distance axis — die Nähe, weit, fern, quer, entlang.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We at the back here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir hinten heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Richtung II: hinten, Norden, Osten, Westen, Süden.

hinten.context_translation: The toilet is at the back on the left.
hinten.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hindanē — the same hind root as English behind and hind; German shifted d to t (the entry points to hinter for the consonantism). [wiktionary]

norden.context_translation: In the north it often rains.
norden.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from Nord, the twin of north; used with im for in the north. [wiktionary]

osten.context_phrase: Der Wind kommt aus dem Osten.
osten.context_translation: The wind comes from the east.
osten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą — the same root as English east, ultimately from the dawn root *ausos, as in Latin aurora. [wiktionary]

westen.context_phrase: Die Sonne geht im Westen unter.
westen.context_translation: The sun sets in the west.
westen.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from West, the twin of west; used with im for in the west. [wiktionary]

süden.context_phrase: Im Süden ist die Sonne stärker.
süden.context_translation: In the south the sun is stronger.
süden.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German süden, ultimately Proto-Germanic *sunþanē — the old noun *sunþrą gave both English south and German Süd (th → d). [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

kirche.etymology_derivation: Greek kyriakon → Scottish kirk / German Kirche.

brücke.context_phrase: Die alte Brücke ist aus Stein.
brücke.context_translation: The old bridge is made of stone.
brücke.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *bruggju — the page lists English bridge as the cognate; German keeps the hard k where English softened to dg. [wiktionary]

links.context_translation: The bank is on the left.
links.etymology_derivation: Middle High German linkes; only Dutch links is a cognate — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

rechts.context_translation: The car is on the right.
rechts.etymology_derivation: recht + adverbial -s; recht is the direct cognate of English right (Recht, already known). [wiktionary]

geradeaus.context_phrase: Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ecke.
geradeaus.context_translation: Go straight ahead to the corner.
geradeaus.etymology_derivation: gerade + aus fused into one adverb; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

eins.context_translation: I have only one of those.
eins.etymology_derivation: Contraction of eines, Proto-Germanic *ainaz — the twin of English one (see ein). [wiktionary]

vier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *feuwar — the direct twin of English four. [wiktionary]

zehn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *tehun — the twin of English ten with the classic t → z shift. [wiktionary]

haustür.context_phrase: Der Schlüssel steckt in der Haustür.
haustür.context_translation: The key is in the front door.
haustür.etymology_derivation: Compound of Haus and Tür; Tür corresponds to English door via the d to t shift, the textbook pair of the dental shift. [wiktionary]

teich.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tīh, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, a doublet of Deich. English ditch and dike are the listed cognates, keeping the d where German shifted to t. [wiktionary]

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. This explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.
